solution:
(1) \(\angle CAB = 90^\circ\).
Line AB is a tangent at A and seg CA is the radius through the point of contact A, and the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius at that point ..... tangent theorem.

(2) The distance of point C from line AB is 6 cm.
The distance of a point from a line is the length of the perpendicular segment from the point to the line. Here seg CA \(\perp\) line AB, so that distance is CA, which is the radius, 6 cm.

(3) In \(\triangle CAB\), \(\angle CAB = 90^\circ\),
\(\therefore BC^2 = CA^2 + AB^2\) ..... Pythagoras theorem
\(= 6^2 + 6^2 = 36 + 36 = 72\)
\(\therefore d(\text{B},\text{C}) = \sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}\) cm.

(4) \(\angle ABC = 45^\circ\).
In \(\triangle CAB\), CA = AB = 6, so it is an isosceles right angled triangle; its two acute angles are congruent and add up to \(90^\circ\), so each is \(45^\circ\) ..... isosceles triangle theorem.

(1) seg OM is a radius and seg RM is a tangent segment, so \(\angle OMR = 90^\circ\) ..... tangent theorem.
In \(\triangle OMR\), \(RM^2 = OR^2 - OM^2 = 10^2 - 5^2 = 100 - 25 = 75\)
\(\therefore RM = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\) cm.
Also RN = RM = \(5\sqrt{3}\) cm ..... tangent segments drawn from an external point to a circle are congruent.
\(\therefore\) the length of each tangent segment is \(5\sqrt{3}\) cm.

(2) In right angled \(\triangle OMR\),
\(\sin \angle MRO = \dfrac{OM}{OR} = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(\therefore \angle MRO = 30^\circ\).

(3) seg OR bisects \(\angle MRN\) (see Q.3 of this Practice set),
\(\therefore \angle MRN = 2 \times \angle MRO = 2 \times 30^\circ = 60^\circ\).

In \(\triangle OMR\) and \(\triangle ONR\),

\(\angle OMR \cong \angle ONR\) ..... each is \(90^\circ\), tangent theorem

hypotenuse OR \(\cong\) hypotenuse OR ..... common side

side OM \(\cong\) side ON ..... radii of the same circle

\(\therefore \triangle OMR \cong \triangle ONR\) ..... hypotenuse-side test

\(\therefore \angle MRO \cong \angle NRO\) and \(\angle MOR \cong \angle NOR\) ..... corresponding angles of congruent triangles

\(\therefore\) ray RO lies in the interior of \(\angle MRN\) and divides it into two congruent angles, and ray OR lies in the interior of \(\angle MON\) and divides it into two congruent angles.

\(\therefore\) seg OR bisects \(\angle MRN\) as well as \(\angle MON\).

The distance between the two parallel tangents is 9 cm.

Justification : Let line \(a\) and line \(b\) be parallel tangents of the circle with centre O, touching it at P and Q respectively.

As proved in the solved example on printed p.54, when two tangents of a circle are parallel their points of contact are the end points of a diameter, so seg PQ is a diameter.

seg OP \(\perp\) line \(a\) and seg OQ \(\perp\) line \(b\) ..... tangent theorem, so seg PQ is the common perpendicular to the two parallel lines, and the distance between two parallel lines is measured along their common perpendicular.

\(\therefore\) the required distance \(= PQ = 2 \times \text{radius} = 2 \times 4.5 = 9\) cm.

When two circles touch each other internally, the distance between their centres is equal to the difference of their radii.

\(\therefore\) distance between the centres \(= 4.8 - 3.5 = 1.3\) cm.

When two circles touch each other externally, the distance between their centres is equal to the sum of their radii.

\(\therefore\) distance between the centres \(= 5.5 + 4.2 = 9.7\) cm.

This is a drawing question; the book prints no answer for it. The two figures are drawn as follows.

(i) Touching externally : the distance between the centres is the sum of the radii, \(4 + 2.8 = 6.8\) cm. So take points A and B with \(d(\text{A},\text{B}) = 6.8\) cm, draw a circle with centre A and radius 4 cm and a circle with centre B and radius 2.8 cm. They touch at the point of seg AB which is 4 cm from A and 2.8 cm from B, and the line through that point perpendicular to seg AB is their common tangent.

(ii) Touching internally : the distance between the centres is the difference of the radii, \(4 - 2.8 = 1.2\) cm. So take points A and B with \(d(\text{A},\text{B}) = 1.2\) cm, draw a circle with centre A and radius 4 cm and a circle with centre B and radius 2.8 cm. The smaller circle lies inside the bigger one and they touch at the point on ray AB at a distance 4 cm from A.

The circles with centres P and Q touch each other at R,
\(\therefore\) points P, R, Q are collinear ..... theorem of touching circles.
Also A, R, B are collinear ..... given (the line through R meets the circles at A and B).

(1) In \(\triangle PAR\), seg PA \(\cong\) seg PR ..... radii of the same circle
\(\therefore \angle PAR \cong \angle PRA\) ..... isosceles triangle theorem ..... (I)

In \(\triangle QRB\), seg QR \(\cong\) seg QB ..... radii of the same circle
\(\therefore \angle QRB \cong \angle QBR\) ..... isosceles triangle theorem ..... (II)

\(\angle PRA \cong \angle QRB\) ..... vertically opposite angles ..... (III)

From (I), (II) and (III), \(\angle PAR \cong \angle QBR\).
These are a pair of alternate angles made by transversal AB with seg AP and seg BQ.
\(\therefore\) seg AP \(\parallel\) seg BQ ..... alternate angles test.

(2) In \(\triangle APR\) and \(\triangle RQB\),
\(\angle PAR \cong \angle QRB\) ..... from (I) and (III)
\(\angle APR \cong \angle RQB\) ..... the remaining angles of the two isosceles triangles, each being \(180^\circ - 2\angle PAR\)
\(\therefore \triangle APR \sim \triangle RQB\) ..... AA test of similarity.

(3) \(\angle PAR = 35^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle PRA = 35^\circ\) ..... from (I)
In \(\triangle PAR\), \(\angle APR = 180^\circ - (35^\circ + 35^\circ) = 110^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle RQB = \angle APR = 110^\circ\) ..... corresponding angles of similar triangles.

Radii AC = 4 cm and BD = 6 cm, and the circles touch externally at E,
\(\therefore AB = AE + EB = 4 + 6 = 10\) cm ..... theorem of touching circles.

Line \(l\) touches the circles at C and D,
\(\therefore\) seg AC \(\perp\) line \(l\) and seg BD \(\perp\) line \(l\) ..... tangent theorem
\(\therefore\) seg AC \(\parallel\) seg BD.

Draw seg AF \(\perp\) seg BD, with F on seg BD.
Then \(\square\)ACDF has four right angles, so it is a rectangle.
\(\therefore CD = AF\) and \(DF = AC = 4\) cm.
\(\therefore BF = BD - DF = 6 - 4 = 2\) cm.

In right angled \(\triangle AFB\),
\(AF^2 = AB^2 - BF^2 = 10^2 - 2^2 = 100 - 4 = 96\)
\(\therefore AF = \sqrt{96} = 4\sqrt{6}\)

\(\therefore CD = 4\sqrt{6}\) cm.

\(\angle ECF\) is a central angle and it intercepts arc EF,
\(\therefore m(\text{arc EF}) = \angle ECF = 70^\circ\) ..... definition of measure of an arc.

D and F are the end points of arc DGF, so arc DGF and arc DEF together make the complete circle.
\(\therefore m(\text{arc DEF}) = 360^\circ - m(\text{arc DGF}) = 360^\circ - 200^\circ = 160^\circ\)

Point E is the only point common to arc DE and arc EF,
\(\therefore m(\text{arc DE}) + m(\text{arc EF}) = m(\text{arc DEF})\) ..... property of sum of measures of arcs
\(\therefore m(\text{arc DE}) + 70^\circ = 160^\circ\)
\(\therefore m(\text{arc DE}) = 90^\circ\)

\(\therefore m(\text{arc DE}) = 90^\circ\) and \(m(\text{arc DEF}) = 160^\circ\).

(1) \(\triangle QRS\) is an equilateral triangle ..... given
\(\therefore\) chord QR \(\cong\) chord RS \(\cong\) chord QS ..... sides of an equilateral triangle
\(\therefore\) arc QR \(\cong\) arc RS \(\cong\) arc QS ..... corresponding arcs of congruent chords of a circle are congruent
\(\therefore\) arc RS \(\cong\) arc QS \(\cong\) arc QR.

(2) The three arcs QR, RS and SQ have only their end points in common and together they make the complete circle,
\(\therefore m(\text{arc QR}) + m(\text{arc RS}) + m(\text{arc SQ}) = 360^\circ\)
From (1) the three measures are equal,
\(\therefore 3 \times m(\text{arc QR}) = 360^\circ\)
\(\therefore m(\text{arc QR}) = m(\text{arc RS}) = m(\text{arc SQ}) = 120^\circ\)

Point R is the only point common to arc QR and arc RS,
\(\therefore m(\text{arc QRS}) = m(\text{arc QR}) + m(\text{arc RS})\) ..... property of sum of measures of arcs
\(= 120^\circ + 120^\circ = 240^\circ\)

chord AB \(\cong\) chord CD ..... given

\(\therefore\) arc ACB \(\cong\) arc CBD ..... corresponding arcs of congruent chords of a circle are congruent. (A chord cuts the circle into two arcs; in figure 3.39 the arcs taken are the ones shown, arc ACB for chord AB and arc CBD for chord CD.)

\(\therefore m(\text{arc ACB}) = m(\text{arc CBD})\)

Point C is the only point common to arc AC and arc CB, and point B is the only point common to arc CB and arc BD,

\(\therefore m(\text{arc AC}) + m(\text{arc CB}) = m(\text{arc CB}) + m(\text{arc BD})\) ..... property of sum of measures of arcs

\(\therefore m(\text{arc AC}) = m(\text{arc BD})\)

These are arcs of the same circle, so they have equal radii as well as equal measures.

\(\therefore\) arc AC \(\cong\) arc BD.

seg OA and seg OB are radii and chord AB is equal to the radius,
\(\therefore OA = OB = AB\), so \(\triangle OAB\) is an equilateral triangle.

(1) \(\angle AOB = 60^\circ\) ..... each angle of an equilateral triangle is \(60^\circ\).

(2) \(\angle ACB\) is an inscribed angle and it intercepts arc AB,
\(\therefore \angle ACB = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc AB}) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 60^\circ = 30^\circ\) ..... inscribed angle theorem.

(3) \(\angle AOB\) is the central angle corresponding to arc AB,
\(\therefore m(\text{arc AB}) = \angle AOB = 60^\circ\) ..... definition of measure of an arc.

(4) \(m(\text{arc ACB}) = 360^\circ - m(\text{arc AB}) = 360^\circ - 60^\circ = 300^\circ\) ..... measure of a major arc.

(1) \(\square\)PQRS is cyclic,
\(\therefore \angle PSR + \angle PQR = 180^\circ\) ..... opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary
\(\therefore 110^\circ + \angle PQR = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle PQR = 70^\circ\)

(2) \(\angle PSR\) is an inscribed angle and it intercepts arc PQR,
\(\therefore \angle PSR = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc PQR})\) ..... inscribed angle theorem
\(\therefore m(\text{arc PQR}) = 2 \times 110^\circ = 220^\circ\)

(3) side PQ \(\cong\) side RQ ..... given
\(\therefore\) arc PQ \(\cong\) arc QR ..... corresponding arcs of congruent chords
\(\therefore m(\text{arc PQ}) = m(\text{arc QR})\)
But \(m(\text{arc PQ}) + m(\text{arc QR}) = m(\text{arc PQR}) = 220^\circ\) ..... property of sum of measures of arcs
\(\therefore 2 \times m(\text{arc QR}) = 220^\circ\)
\(\therefore m(\text{arc QR}) = 110^\circ\)

(4) \(\angle PRQ\) is an inscribed angle and it intercepts arc PQ,
\(\therefore \angle PRQ = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\text{arc PQ}) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 110^\circ = 55^\circ\) ..... inscribed angle theorem.

\(\square\)MRPN is cyclic and \(\angle R\), \(\angle N\) are its opposite angles,
\(\therefore \angle R + \angle N = 180^\circ\) ..... opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary

\(\therefore (5x - 13) + (4x + 4) = 180\)
\(\therefore 9x - 9 = 180\)
\(\therefore 9x = 189\)
\(\therefore x = 21\)

\(\therefore \angle R = (5 \times 21 - 13)^\circ = (105 - 13)^\circ = 92^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle N = (4 \times 21 + 4)^\circ = (84 + 4)^\circ = 88^\circ\)

Check : \(92^\circ + 88^\circ = 180^\circ\).

Point T lies in the exterior of the circle and R, S lie on it. In figure 3.58 seg TR crosses the circle; let it intersect the circle in the point M other than R.

seg RS is a diameter of the circle,
\(\therefore \angle RMS = 90^\circ\) ..... angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

Now T-M-R, so \(\angle RMS\) is an exterior angle of \(\triangle TMS\) at M,
\(\therefore \angle RMS = \angle MTS + \angle MST\) ..... exterior angle theorem of a triangle.

\(\angle MST\) is an angle of a triangle, so \(\angle MST > 0\),
\(\therefore \angle MTS < \angle RMS = 90^\circ\)

But \(\angle MTS\) and \(\angle RTS\) are the same angle, since M lies on seg TR.

\(\therefore \angle RTS < 90^\circ\), that is \(\angle RTS\) is an acute angle.

Let \(\square\)ABCD be any rectangle.

Each angle of a rectangle is a right angle,
\(\therefore \angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90^\circ\)

\(\therefore \angle A + \angle C = 90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\)

So one pair of opposite angles of \(\square\)ABCD is supplementary.

\(\therefore \square\)ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral ..... converse of cyclic quadrilateral theorem.

\(\therefore\) any rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral.

seg YZ and seg XT are altitudes of \(\triangle WXY\) intersecting at P,
\(\therefore\) seg YZ \(\perp\) side WX and seg XT \(\perp\) side WY.

(1) In \(\square\)WZPT,
\(\angle WZP = 90^\circ\) ..... seg YZ \(\perp\) side WX and P lies on seg YZ
\(\angle WTP = 90^\circ\) ..... seg XT \(\perp\) side WY and P lies on seg XT
\(\angle WZP\) and \(\angle WTP\) are opposite angles of \(\square\)WZPT and
\(\angle WZP + \angle WTP = 90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore \square\)WZPT is cyclic ..... converse of cyclic quadrilateral theorem.

(2) \(\angle XZY = 90^\circ\) ..... seg YZ \(\perp\) side WX, and Z lies on side WX
\(\angle XTY = 90^\circ\) ..... seg XT \(\perp\) side WY, and T lies on side WY

So seg XY subtends equal angles (each \(90^\circ\)) at the two distinct points Z and T, and Z, T lie on the same side of line XY.

\(\therefore\) points X, Z, T, Y are concyclic ..... if two points on a given line subtend equal angles at two distinct points which lie on the same side of the line, then the four points are concyclic.

In figure 3.60, point M lies in the exterior of the circle and the two secants through M cut the circle at E, N and at F, S.

\(\therefore \angle NMS = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc NS}) - m(\text{arc EF})\right]\) ..... if two lines containing chords of a circle intersect each other outside the circle, the measure of the angle between them is half the difference in measures of the arcs intercepted by the angle

\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[125^\circ - 37^\circ\right]\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 88^\circ = 44^\circ\)

\(\therefore \angle NMS = 44^\circ\)

Chords AC and DE intersect each other at point B in the interior of the circle.
\(\angle ABE\) intercepts arc AE and its opposite angle \(\angle DBC\) intercepts arc DC.

\(\therefore \angle ABE = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[m(\text{arc AE}) + m(\text{arc DC})\right]\) ..... if two chords of a circle intersect each other in the interior of the circle, the measure of the angle between them is half the sum of the measures of the arcs intercepted by the angle and its opposite angle

\(\therefore 108^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[95^\circ + m(\text{arc DC})\right]\)

\(\therefore 216^\circ = 95^\circ + m(\text{arc DC})\)

\(\therefore m(\text{arc DC}) = 121^\circ\)

Ray PQ touches the circle at Q and line PS is a secant cutting the circle at R and S, with P-R-S.

\(\therefore PQ^2 = PR \times PS\) ..... tangent secant segments theorem

\(\therefore 12^2 = 8 \times PS\)

\(\therefore 144 = 8 \times PS\)

\(\therefore PS = 18\)

Now P-R-S, \(\therefore RS = PS - PR = 18 - 8 = 10\)

\(\therefore PS = 18\) and \(RS = 10\).

Chord MN and chord RS intersect each other at point D in the interior of the circle,
\(\therefore MD \times DN = RD \times DS\) ..... theorem of internal division of chords.

(1) \(8 \times DN = 15 \times 4\)
\(\therefore 8 \times DN = 60\)
\(\therefore DN = 7.5\)

(2) \(MD \times DN = 9 \times 8 = 72\)
\(\therefore RD \times DS = 72\)
Also R-D-S, \(\therefore RD + DS = RS = 18\), so \(RD = 18 - DS\).
\(\therefore (18 - DS) \times DS = 72\)
\(\therefore DS^2 - 18\,DS + 72 = 0\)
\(\therefore (DS - 6)(DS - 12) = 0\)
\(\therefore DS = 6\) or \(DS = 12\)

\(\therefore DS = 12\) or \(DS = 6\) (both are possible, according to which of the two segments of chord RS the point D cuts off).

seg AB is a tangent segment touching the circle at B, and line AD is a secant cutting the circle at C and D, with A-C-D.

(1) \(AB^2 = AC \times AD\) ..... tangent secant segments theorem
\(\therefore 12^2 = 8 \times AD\)
\(\therefore 144 = 8 \times AD\)
\(\therefore AD = 18\)

(2) A-C-D, \(\therefore DC = AD - AC = 18 - 8 = 10\)

(3) seg DC is a chord of the circle and seg OE \(\perp\) seg AD, that is seg OE \(\perp\) chord DC,
\(\therefore\) E is the midpoint of chord DC ..... the perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to its chord bisects the chord
\(\therefore DE = \dfrac{1}{2} \times DC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 = 5\)

In figure 3.80 the two secants through P cut the circle at Q, R and at S, T, with P-Q-R and P-S-T.

\(PR = PQ + QR = 6 + 10 = 16\)

\(PQ \times PR = PS \times PT\) ..... theorem of external division of chords

\(\therefore 6 \times 16 = 8 \times PT\)

\(\therefore 96 = 8 \times PT\)

\(\therefore PT = 12\)

Now P-S-T, \(\therefore TS = PT - PS = 12 - 8 = 4\)

\(\therefore TS = 4\)

seg EF is a diameter and seg DF is a tangent segment touching the circle at F,
\(\therefore\) seg DF \(\perp\) seg EF ..... tangent theorem
\(\therefore \angle DFE = 90^\circ\), so \(\triangle DFE\) is a right angled triangle with hypotenuse DE.

G lies on the circle and seg EF is a diameter,
\(\therefore \angle EGF = 90^\circ\) ..... angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle
\(\therefore\) seg FG \(\perp\) seg DE, that is seg FG is the altitude on the hypotenuse of \(\triangle DFE\).

In \(\triangle EGF\) and \(\triangle EFD\),
\(\angle EGF \cong \angle EFD\) ..... each is \(90^\circ\)
\(\angle GEF \cong \angle FED\) ..... common angle
\(\therefore \triangle EGF \sim \triangle EFD\) ..... AA test of similarity
\(\therefore \dfrac{EG}{EF} = \dfrac{EF}{ED}\) ..... corresponding sides of similar triangles
\(\therefore EF^2 = EG \times ED\)

But seg EF is a diameter and the radius is \(r\), so \(EF = 2r\).

\(\therefore (2r)^2 = GE \times DE\)

\(\therefore DE \times GE = 4r^2\)

[Textbook note: sub-part (3) as printed gives \(d(\text{PQ}) = 15\) cm while asking for the locations of a point R that is nowhere located, and prints "are line on line \(l\)" for "are there on line \(l\)". The printed answer key (2 locations, 12 cm) follows only if the given distance is \(d(\text{O},\text{R}) = 15\) cm, and that is the reading used below.]

(1) \(d(\text{O},\text{P}) = 9\) cm.
Line \(l\) touches the circle at P, so seg OP is the radius drawn to the point of contact, and the radius of the circle is 9 cm.

(2) \(d(\text{O},\text{Q}) = 8\) cm and the radius is 9 cm, so \(d(\text{O},\text{Q}) < \) radius.
\(\therefore\) point Q lies in the interior of the circle.

(3) Let R be a point on line \(l\) with \(d(\text{O},\text{R}) = 15\) cm.
seg OP \(\perp\) line \(l\) ..... tangent theorem, so \(\angle OPR = 90^\circ\).
In right angled \(\triangle OPR\),
\(PR^2 = OR^2 - OP^2 = 15^2 - 9^2 = 225 - 81 = 144\)
\(\therefore PR = 12\) cm.
On line \(l\) there is one such point on each side of P.
\(\therefore\) there are 2 locations of point R, and each of them is at a distance of 12 cm from point P.

seg KL is a tangent segment touching the circle at L and seg ML is a radius,
\(\therefore \angle MLK = 90^\circ\) ..... tangent theorem.

(1) In right angled \(\triangle MLK\),
\(ML^2 = MK^2 - KL^2 = 12^2 - (6\sqrt{3})^2 = 144 - 108 = 36\)
\(\therefore ML = 6\)
\(\therefore\) the radius of the circle is 6 units.

(2) In right angled \(\triangle MLK\),
\(\sin \angle K = \dfrac{ML}{MK} = \dfrac{6}{12} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(\therefore \angle K = 30^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle M = 180^\circ - (90^\circ + 30^\circ) = 60^\circ\)

\(\therefore \angle K = 30^\circ\) and \(\angle M = 60^\circ\).

seg AB and seg AC are tangent segments touching the circle at B and C,
\(\therefore \angle ABO = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle ACO = 90^\circ\) ..... tangent theorem ..... (I)

seg AB \(\cong\) seg AC ..... tangent segments drawn from an external point to a circle are congruent
seg OB \(\cong\) seg OC ..... radii of the same circle, each \(= r\)
and \(l(\text{AB}) = r\) ..... given

\(\therefore AB = BO = OC = CA = r\)

\(\therefore\) in \(\square\)ABOC all four sides are congruent, so \(\square\)ABOC is a rhombus ..... (II)

From (I), \(\square\)ABOC is a rhombus having a right angle.

\(\therefore \square\)ABOC is a square.

E, F, G, H are the points at which the circle touches sides AB, BC, CD, DA of \(\square\)ABCD.

Tangent segments drawn to a circle from an external point are congruent,
\(\therefore AE = AH\), \(BE = BF\), \(CF = CG\) and \(DG = DH\).

\(\therefore AB + CD = (AE + EB) + (CG + GD)\)
\(= (AH + BF) + (CF + DH)\)
\(= (AH + HD) + (BF + FC)\)
\(= AD + BC\) ..... (I)

\(\square\)ABCD is a parallelogram,
\(\therefore AB = CD\) and \(AD = BC\) ..... opposite sides of a parallelogram ..... (II)

From (I) and (II), \(2AB = 2AD\), \(\therefore AD = AB\).

Now \(AB = AE + EB = 4.5 + 5.5 = 10\)

\(\therefore AD = 10\)

(The parallelogram is therefore a rhombus, which is what Problem set 3 Q.1(3) states.)

(1) T lies on the circle with centre M and MT is a radius of that circle,
\(\therefore MT = 9\) cm.

(2) The circle with centre N touches the circle with centre M internally at T,
\(\therefore\) the distance between the centres is the difference of the radii,
\(\therefore MN = 9 - 2.5 = 6.5\) cm.

(3) Radius RM of the bigger circle touches the smaller circle at S, so seg NS is the radius of the smaller circle drawn to the point of contact S,
\(\therefore \angle NSM = 90^\circ\) ..... tangent theorem.

Hence, in right angled \(\triangle NSM\),
\(MS^2 = MN^2 - NS^2 = (6.5)^2 - (2.5)^2 = 42.25 - 6.25 = 36\)
\(\therefore MS = 6\) cm.

M-S-R, \(\therefore SR = MR - MS = 9 - 6 = 3\) cm.

\(\therefore MS : SR = 6 : 3 = 2 : 1\)

The book prints this proof with blanks; the completed proof is given below.

Construction : Draw segments XZ and YZ.

Proof : By theorem of touching circles, points X, Z, Y are collinear.

\(\therefore \angle XZA \cong \angle BZY\) ..... opposite angles (vertically opposite angles, as A-Z-B and X-Z-Y)

Let \(\angle XZA = \angle BZY = a\) ..... (I)

Now, seg XA \(\cong\) seg XZ ..... (radii of the same circle)

\(\therefore \angle XAZ = \angle XZA = a\) ..... (isosceles triangle theorem) (II)

similarly, seg YB \(\cong\) seg YZ ..... (radii of the same circle)

\(\therefore \angle BZY = \angle ZBY = a\) ..... (isosceles triangle theorem) (III)

\(\therefore\) from (I), (II), (III),

\(\angle XAZ = \angle ZBY\)

\(\therefore\) radius XA \(\parallel\) radius YB ..... (alternate angles test, the alternate angles being made by transversal AB)

The circles with centres X and Y touch each other internally at Z,
\(\therefore\) points X, Y, Z are collinear ..... theorem of touching circles.
Since the contact is internal, ray ZX and ray ZY are the same ray.

Also B-A-Z ..... given (seg BZ is a chord of the bigger circle intersecting the smaller circle at A).

In \(\triangle XAZ\), seg XA \(\cong\) seg XZ ..... radii of the smaller circle
\(\therefore \angle XAZ \cong \angle XZA\) ..... isosceles triangle theorem ..... (I)

In \(\triangle YBZ\), seg YB \(\cong\) seg YZ ..... radii of the bigger circle
\(\therefore \angle YBZ \cong \angle YZB\) ..... isosceles triangle theorem ..... (II)

\(\angle XZA\) and \(\angle YZB\) are the same angle, because ray ZX is the same as ray ZY and ray ZA is the same as ray ZB.
\(\therefore \angle XZA \cong \angle YZB\) ..... (III)

From (I), (II) and (III), \(\angle XAZ \cong \angle YBZ\).

These are a pair of corresponding angles made by transversal BZ with seg AX and seg BY.

\(\therefore\) seg AX \(\parallel\) seg BY ..... corresponding angles test.

Let the radius of the circle be \(r\), so \(OP = OR = r\).

Line \(l\) touches the circle at P, \(\therefore\) seg OP \(\perp\) line \(l\) ..... tangent theorem.
chord RS \(\parallel\) line \(l\) ..... given
\(\therefore\) seg OP \(\perp\) chord RS, and the chord RS passes through Q, so seg OQ \(\perp\) chord RS.

\(\therefore\) Q is the midpoint of chord RS ..... the perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to its chord bisects the chord
\(\therefore RQ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times RS = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 = 6\)

Q is the midpoint of radius OP,
\(\therefore OQ = \dfrac{r}{2}\)

In right angled \(\triangle OQR\),
\(OR^2 = OQ^2 + QR^2\) ..... Pythagoras theorem
\(\therefore r^2 = \left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)^2 + 6^2\)
\(\therefore r^2 = \dfrac{r^2}{4} + 36\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{3r^2}{4} = 36\)
\(\therefore r^2 = 48\)
\(\therefore r = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\)

\(\therefore\) the radius of the circle is \(4\sqrt{3}\) cm.

Line PQ touches the circle at T and seg CT is the radius through the point of contact,
\(\therefore\) seg CT \(\perp\) line PQ ..... tangent theorem.

Also seg AP \(\perp\) line PQ and seg BQ \(\perp\) line PQ ..... given.

Suppose, if possible, that three points A, B, C on a circle are collinear.

Then the line containing A, B and C has three distinct points in common with the circle.

But a line and a circle can have at most two points in common : a line that does not meet a circle has no common point, a tangent has exactly one common point, and a secant has exactly two common points.

This contradicts the supposition.

\(\therefore\) our supposition is wrong.

\(\therefore\) any three points on a circle cannot be collinear.

(The same result also follows from the fact that if A, B, C were collinear the perpendicular bisectors of seg AB and seg BC would both be perpendicular to the same line, hence parallel, so they would never intersect and no point equidistant from A, B and C would exist.)
